lede: Two ways to beat a pathogen: kill it with a drug, or train your body before it arrives. Antibiotics do the first, for bacteria only, and overusing them breeds bacteria they cannot kill. Vaccines do the second, by leaving memory behind.
can: Explain what antibiotics do, why they fail against viruses, and read a plate of clear zones.
Explain resistance as natural selection, and how hospitals keep superbugs such as MRSA down.
Describe how a vaccine and a booster protect you, and read an antibody graph.

md: In 1928 a mould landed on one of Alexander Fleming's dishes of bacteria, and the bacteria near it died. The chemical the mould made, penicillin, became one of the first antibiotics. Bacteria are now fighting back, and vaccines stop some diseases before they can start.

md: An **antibiotic** is a chemical made by fungi, such as **penicillin**, used against diseases caused by bacteria. It either **kills the bacteria** or **stops them growing**. Many antibiotics attack the cell wall, which only bacteria have, as in the drawing. A virus has no cell wall and reproduces inside your own cells, so antibiotics do nothing against colds, flu or HIV.

prompt: Which of these diseases could be treated with an antibiotic?
explain: An antibiotic acts only on bacteria, attacking parts such as the cell wall that a virus does not have. Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium; flu and colds are caused by viruses, which hide inside your own cells. The answer is tuberculosis.

md: To test antibiotics, bacteria are spread over agar and paper discs soaked in antibiotic are laid on top. Where an antibiotic works, it kills the bacteria round its disc and leaves a **clear zone**. The **largest** clear zone marks the most effective antibiotic; **no zone** means the bacteria are resistant to it. In the drawing, A is the most effective and C does not work.

title: Say which is biggest
md: On the Summer 2025 practical paper, most candidates picked the right antibiotic, but many lost the marks for the reason. The reason needs the comparison in words: it had the largest clear zone, so it killed the most bacteria.

prompt: On one plate, antibiotic A gives a clear zone 26 mm across, antibiotic B one 15 mm across, and antibiotic C none. Which answer earns the marks for choosing the most effective antibiotic?
options: A, because it had the largest clear zone, so it killed the most bacteria
A, because it had a big clear zone
C, because the bacteria grew right up to it
answer: A, because it had the largest clear zone, so it killed the most bacteria
explain: A clear zone is where bacteria were killed, so the widest zone marks the antibiotic that killed the most. With three to compare, 'a big clear zone' could describe any of them: the mark needs 'largest', and what it means. C killed none. The answer is A, because it had the largest clear zone, so it killed the most bacteria.

md:
**Which antibiotic affects all three types?** X: it has a clear zone on every plate.
**Which is most effective against bacteria A?** Y: it has the **largest** clear zone on plate A, so it killed the most bacteria.
**Which types is Z not effective against?** A and B: there is no clear zone round Z on either plate.

**Are any of these bacteria MRSA?** Answer from the plates, not from what you know about MRSA in general. Every type has a clear zone round at least one antibiotic, so each one can be killed by an antibiotic, and none behaves like a superbug.

prompt: Using the three plates in the drawing, which antibiotic should be chosen to treat an infection by bacteria C?
explain: Compare the clear zones on plate C only, because that is the infection being treated. The antibiotic with the largest clear zone there killed the most of those bacteria: X's zone on plate C is 17 mm across, against 13 mm for Z and 10 mm for Y. The answer is X.

md: In any population of bacteria there is variation: by chance, a **mutation** makes a few resistant to an antibiotic. The antibiotic kills the bacteria that are not resistant; the resistant ones **survive**, **reproduce** and pass on the gene for resistance. So every dose raises the proportion that are resistant: in the drawing, 10%, then 35%, then 70%, then 95%.

title: Why it is selection, not immunity
md: Bacteria have no immune system and make no antibodies. The antibiotic does not create resistance either: the resistant bacteria were there before it was used. It only removes the ones that are not resistant, which leaves the resistant ones to multiply.

prompt: In the population of bacteria in the drawing, why did the percentage that were resistant rise from generation 1 to generation 4?
options: The resistant ones survived each dose and reproduced
The antibiotic made the bacteria resistant
The bacteria made antibodies against the antibiotic
answer: The resistant ones survived each dose and reproduced
explain: Look at generation 1: two bacteria were already resistant before any dose. Each dose killed most of the others, while the resistant ones survived and reproduced, so each new generation held more of them. Nothing was made resistant, and bacteria make no antibodies. The answer is that the resistant ones survived each dose and reproduced.

md: Every unnecessary use of an antibiotic gives resistant bacteria another chance to take over. A **superbug** is a bacterium resistant to most antibiotics; **MRSA** is one. It is hard to get rid of because few antibiotics treat it, it spreads on hands, clothes and surfaces, and hospital patients are often already weak.

Hospitals reduce superbugs with **hand hygiene** between patients, **isolating** infected patients, gloves and gowns, disinfecting wards, and prescribing antibiotics only when they are needed. Outside the body, MRSA is killed by **alcohol hand gel**, antiseptics and disinfectants. In the graph, hospital A's cases fell after its campaign began.

prompt: Which of these would kill MRSA bacteria on a nurse's hands?
explain: MRSA is resistant to most antibiotics, so penicillin is exactly what fails against it, and a vaccine prepares a body rather than killing anything on skin. Outside the body, MRSA is killed by chemicals that destroy any bacteria: alcohol gel, antiseptics, disinfectants. The answer is alcohol hand gel.

md: A **vaccine** contains a **modified** form of a pathogen, dead or weakened, so it cannot make you ill. **Lymphocytes**, a kind of white blood cell, recognise its antigens and make **antibodies** against them. Some become **memory lymphocytes**, which stay in the blood. So a vaccine raises the levels of antibodies and memory lymphocytes in the blood.

Months later the real pathogen arrives. The memory lymphocytes recognise it at once, so antibodies are made **faster** and in **greater numbers** than the first time, and the pathogen is destroyed before you feel ill.

prompt: After a vaccination, which cells stay in the blood and recognise the real pathogen later? Memory ______.
answer: lymphocytes | lymphocyte | cells | memory lymphocytes | memory cells | white blood cells
explain: The vaccine's modified pathogen makes lymphocytes produce antibodies, and some of those lymphocytes become memory lymphocytes that stay in the blood. When the real pathogen arrives, they recognise it and trigger a fast, large response. The answer is memory lymphocytes.

title: Antibody, antibiotic or vaccine?
md: An **antibody** is a protein your own lymphocytes make. An **antibiotic** is a drug, made by fungi, that kills bacteria. A **vaccine** is an injection of a modified pathogen. Examiners have found antibodies written where the drug is meant, so read the question and match the word to it.

prompt: Which of these is made by your own white blood cells?
explain: Only one of the three comes from inside you: lymphocytes, a kind of white blood cell, make antibodies. An antibiotic is a drug made by fungi, and a vaccine is an injection of a modified pathogen. The answer is an antibody.

alt: A graph of antibody level against time. After the first dose the level rises slowly to a small peak of 24 and falls back without reaching the dashed line at 30; after the booster in week 10 it rises quickly to 120 and stays above the line until week 28.
caption: The dashed line is the level needed for immunity. The booster's response is faster, higher and longer than the first.

md: On an antibody graph, the dashed line marks the level needed for **immunity**. Here the first dose gives a small, slow response that peaks at 24, below the line of 30, so it does not protect on its own. The **booster** meets memory lymphocytes, so the level rises faster and higher, to 120, and stays above the line for longer.

**How many times higher** is the second peak? Divide: 120 ÷ 24 = 5.
**For how long** was the person immune? Subtract the week the curve crossed the line going up from the week it crossed going down: 28 − 10 = about 18 weeks.

prompt: On another antibody graph, the peak after a booster is 90 arbitrary units and the peak after the first dose is 15. How many times higher is the booster's peak?
explain: 'How many times higher' is a division of the larger peak by the smaller, never a subtraction: 90 − 15 = 75 says how much higher, not how many times. 90 ÷ 15 = 6.

15 resistant bacteria, because the others changed
explain: The antibiotic kills every bacterium that is not resistant, so none of those can appear in the drawing. The resistant ones are not killed, and in two days they divide, so there are more than 3. Nothing changes into a resistant bacterium. The answer is only resistant bacteria, more than 3.

md: **A new organism, the same selection.** Snakes resisting a newt's poison, or lice resisting a lotion: explain them exactly as bacteria and an antibiotic. Variation, the others killed, the resistant survive and reproduce, the gene passed on. Never immunity. (Summer 2024 Higher.)
**True, false or cannot tell.** Use only the graph. If the graph cannot show it, such as a year outside its range or what caused a change, the answer is cannot tell. (Summer 2025 Higher.)

explain: A graph shows what happened and when, not why. The fall came after the campaign began, but something else could have changed at the same time, so the graph alone cannot show the cause. The answer is cannot tell.
